item.title: "A Space Where I Can Be Myself": Exploring Safe Visibility for Graduate Student Mothers in Mom Cafes
item.description: arXiv:2611.08710v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graduate student mothers navigate intertwined demands of graduate study and caregiving, yet little is known about how they seek support through online communities. We examine this through Mom Cafes, locally based online parenting communities in South Korea. Drawing on focus group interviews and design workshops with 22 graduate student mothers, we identify a pattern of dual invisibility: caregiving circumstances were difficult to make legible in academic contexts, while academic circumstances were difficult to make legible in parenting contexts. Although Mom Cafes offered useful local information and emotional reassurance, concerns specific to graduate student motherhood were harder to articulate or safely disclose. Participants sought ways to make graduate student motherhood recognizable when relevant, but their designs highlighted tensions around identifiability, judgment, relational burden and accountability. We conceptualize these tensions as safe visibility and discuss infrastructures for selective recognition, low-obligation connection, and accountable pathways to practical care.
item.dc:creator: Jeanne Choi, Joohee Choi, Jeong-woo Jang

item.title: Dynamic signatures of collective knowledge through navigation in a network with semantic structure
item.description: arXiv:2611.08812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What distinguishes how humans navigate an information network like Wikipedia from what the underlying graph structure and language statistics alone predict? To study human collective navigation, we analyze 70,770 human trajectories through Wikispeedia, an online game where players navigate between articles to reach a target. To compare groups of trajectories rather than individual ones, we merge all trajectories leaving or entering a given article into a Flow Tree. Flow Trees compress collections of trajectories into hierarchies of group splits. We build forward and reverse Flow Trees for 815 of the most commonly traversed articles, representing divergence and convergence, respectively. We compare humans against four random-walker null models, either unweighted or weighted by graph structure, word frequency, or semantic similarity to target. Human Flow Trees are deeper with longer trunks and later splits, indicating players stay together longer than random walkers, whose Flow Trees tend to fan out immediately. An article's degree predicts 51.3-70.9% of the variation in Flow Tree branching factor for random walkers, but only 24.1-36.2% for humans. Taking what graph structure fails to predict as a two-dimensional coordinate system, we define four article types (beacons, funnels, forks, and corridors), distinguished by how humans enter and exit them. These human-defined types are not explained by out-degree or title-word frequency are, and are not recovered by any random walker. A fifth null model, built from first-order human click preferences, partially reproduces human Flow Tree shape but differs significantly in how much of that shape degree explains. We consider collective knowledge to be the structure shared by players who never communicate, beyond what graph structure imposes. It comprises first-order click preferences and a significant component that extends across clicks.
item.dc:creator: Abby Bertics, Elizabeth R. Chrastil, Jean M. Carlson

item.title: Research Collaborations Within and Across Disciplines in NIH-Funded Atlas Programs
item.description: arXiv:2611.09741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) fund several programs (aka consortia) that support the construction of organ-specific or whole person atlases. These initiatives are designed to build comprehensive open reference datasets while advancing knowledge graphs, analytics, visualizations, and user interfaces needed to explore multiscale human atlas data. Here, we compare the Human Tumor Atlas Network (HTAN), Human BioMolecular Atlas Program (HuBMAP) and Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet) to examine collaboration by consortium component (CC) and researcher role and its relation to scientific impact. We retrieved 884 NIH award records and identified 1,255 focal publications acknowledging these awards, involving 8,952 researchers; compiled 99,108 citing publications covering 93% of the focal publications; constructed co-authorship networks; and as single-project publications or internal collaborations (IC), including intra-CC and inter-CCs collaborations. within each atlas program. Results show that IC publications are rare but involve many funded projects and principal investigators (PIs). Technology-oriented CCs tend to engage in intra-CC collaboration, whereas experimental-oriented CCs often collaborate across CCs of the same type. Compared with other researchers, PIs exhibited a significantly stronger association with inter-CCs than with single-project publications. IC publications have higher mean Relative Citation Ratios than single-project publications. Inter-CCs publications have significantly higher cumulative and annual citation levels in the first five post-publication years. Study methods and results can be used to inform the funding, management, and impact reporting for future Big Science programs that bring together 300+ experts from different disciplines to address major research challenges.
item.dc:creator: Michael P. Ginda, Yongxin Kong, Katy B\"orner

item.title: StreamTab: Training-Free Temporal Link Prediction with Tabular Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.09052v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Temporal link prediction uses past interactions to predict whether two nodes will interact in the future. Temporal graph neural networks achieve strong results on this task, but they are trained separately for each graph. How a model should use interaction history also depends on the candidates it is compared with. A past interaction can distinguish a recurring link from a random pair that has never interacted, but when the negative candidates have also interacted before, other signals are needed. We propose StreamTab, a training-free framework built on a frozen tabular foundation model pretrained only on synthetic tables. StreamTab describes each candidate pair by statistics of its past interactions and shows the model recent observed interactions and sampled negative pairs as labeled examples, from which the model scores new candidates. Its central design, regime conditioning, samples the negative examples according to how the candidates are sampled, so the examples show the distinction the model must make. As new interactions arrive, StreamTab updates the statistics and refreshes the examples while the model parameters stay fixed. On thirteen datasets against 21 temporal graph baselines, StreamTab achieves the highest average precision on twelve datasets under historical sampling and eleven under inductive sampling, and ranks first or stays within one point of the best on seven datasets under random sampling. With the same features and model, regime conditioning raises average precision over examples with random negatives by a median of 12.6 points under historical sampling.
item.dc:creator: Mingqi Yang, Renqi Wu

item.title: PAGSL: Path-Augmenting Graph Structure Learning for explainable scholar recommendation
item.description: arXiv:2611.09126v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Explainable scholar recommendation aims to identify potential scholars of interest and provide reasonable explanations for the recommendations. However, existing frameworks struggle with optimization-induced noise and "hub node bias", yielding trivial explanations that lack hierarchical depth and personalization. To this end, we propose a novel explainable scholar recommendation model, Path-Augmenting Graph Structure Learning (named PAGSL). PAGSL combines representation learning and semantic path knowledge to ensure recommendation performance while providing interpretable results from two perspectives. Specifically, it activates latent academic paths among entities through graph augmentation and employs a path-based neural network to encode these paths for recommendation. A masking mechanism with path score optimization is designed to generate concise and informative explanations. We evaluate PAGSL on three academic datasets (Scholat, AMiner, and ResearchGate), comprising approximately 49,000 authors and over 330,000 interaction records. Experimental evaluations validate that PAGSL outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving significant improvements of 6.31\% in F1-score, 6.29\% in Accuracy and 5.95\% in AUC for recommendation. Crucially, in terms of explainability, we provide quantitative results and visualization effects. Furthermore, ablation studies validate the effectiveness of our heterogeneous convolution and path representation learning. PAGSL achieves strong performance in both recommendation accuracy and explainability.
item.dc:creator: Jiale Xu, Mingshu Ai, Junjie Huang, Tao Jia

item.title: RoleWalk: training-free structural embeddings for directed graphs that transfer across graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.09189v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Structural role embeddings describe a node by its position in a graph - hub, bridge, periphery, member of a dense core - rather than by who its neighbours are. Existing methods either learn coordinates specific to one graph (struc2vec, Role2Vec, RESD) or read scales and normalisations from the whole graph (GraphWave, Digraphwave), so the same neighbourhood can receive different coordinates in two graphs; few read edge directions. We present RoleWalk, a training-free embedding that follows a short lazy random walk from each node and records, at each step, two distributions: that of the transition probabilities, through its characteristic function at a fixed grid of frequencies, and that of the walker's distance to its starting node. On directed graphs, walks that go forward then backward add who shares a node's targets or sources. The embedding depends only on a node's neighbourhood within a fixed radius, so its coordinates mean the same thing in every graph. We show that, without curvature, it is the kernel mean embedding of the walk's footprint, that it separates graphs that the Weisfeiler-Leman test cannot, and that pruning small probabilities comes with a per-node error certificate. Empirically, RoleWalk is competitive with the best role embeddings on five classification benchmarks at a fraction of their cost, has the highest scores on real directed roles in Wikipedia adminship, exceeds the published accuracy of Digraphwave at every noise level of its own Enron network-alignment benchmark, transfers centrality predictors to graphs four times larger better than existing inductive embeddings, hand-made features and a trained GIN, and embeds a million nodes in 20 s to 3 min on one CPU core. The code is open source (BSD license): https://github.com/kerighan/rolewalk
item.dc:creator: Maixent Chenebaux

item.title: Matrix Factorization Framework for Community Detection under the Degree-Corrected Block Model
item.description: arXiv:2601.06262v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Community detection is a fundamental task in data analysis, and block models provide an approach for identifying diverse community structures. The degree-corrected block model (DCBM) is an established model that captures node degree heterogeneity. However, inference methods are computationally costly and sensitive to initialization, while cheaper alternatives, such as spectral or modularity-based approaches, may be less effective at recovering certain non-assortative structures. In this work, we show that DCBM inference can be reformulated as a constrained nonnegative matrix trifactorization problem. Leveraging this insight, we propose a scalable community detection method with a theoretically grounded initialization providing an initial partition for inference algorithms. Our approach is agnostic to network structure and applies to any graph representable by a DCBM. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmark networks show that our method achieves community recovery comparable to, and sometimes better than, that achieved by the DCBM inference methods, while being faster: it processes a graph with 100,000 nodes and 500,000 edges in about 30 seconds. Moreover, the initialization significantly improves solution quality. Overall, this work provides a scalable and robust framework for community detection and highlights the benefits of a matrix-factorization perspective for the DCBM.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Dache, Arnaud Vandaele, Nicolas Gillis

item.title: False Belief Dissemination, Persistence and Mitigation in Multi-Agent Social Networks Through the Lens of the Mandela Effect
item.description: arXiv:2610.33026v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent social networks are emerging as communities in which agents communicate, retain memories, and publish information that others can find as evidence. These interactions create opportunities for false claims to spread and remain influential beyond their original sources, analogous to the Mandela effect in human societies, in which many people recall the same false memory. In this paper, we systematically study false-belief dynamics through the lens of the Mandela effect, focusing on dissemination, persistence, and mitigation. Specifically, we build a controlled framework connecting agent communication, private memory, and a shared simulated web to mimic information dissemination in practical social networks, supported by 540 fabricated claims spanning 8 domains and 4 plausibility levels. For dissemination, we measure how widely and quickly claims gain acceptance across models and communication topologies. For persistence, we withdraw agents promoting fabricated claims while retaining existing articles and memories, and track subsequent acceptance. For mitigation, we compare preventive measures applied before implantation with corrective interventions introduced after claims have spread. Experimental results show that evaluated models readily accept and disseminate fabricated claims, with dissemination reach as high as 96.0%. Dissemination reach varies with claim plausibility, domain, and network size and composition, while communication topology shapes dissemination speed across model families. Acceptance barely declines after fabricators withdraw, and targeted corrective interventions outperform the preventive measures without eliminating false beliefs. These findings identify persistent false beliefs as a safety challenge for multi-agent social networks and highlight the need to address both their initial dissemination and the accumulated evidence that sustains them.
item.dc:creator: Dianzhi Yu, Hongru Wang, Ziheng Xiong, Yanyu Chen, Zixing Song, Jianting Chen, Zhenfei Yin, Jeff Z. Pan, Amos Storkey, Irwin King

item.title: Revisiting Temporal Link Prediction through Structural Proximity
item.description: arXiv:2610.38385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing temporal link prediction methods typically rely on learned temporal representations to capture evolving interaction patterns. In this paper, we show that a classical structural proximity measure can match or outperform these methods without training or learned temporal sequence modeling. We revisit Personalized PageRank (PPR) on historical interaction graphs, using simple sliding-window retention or exponential time decay. Surprisingly, across 14 datasets, Time-decay PPR ranks first on nine and second on four among the compared methods, including datasets with few repeated edges. To understand this result, we examine the historical paths connecting source nodes to previously unseen destinations. We find that such paths contain useful predictive information, and that PPR outperforms a strong neural baseline on queries where historical structure clearly distinguishes the true destination from negative candidates. These results show that strong performance on current benchmarks does not necessarily require complex temporal models. More fundamentally, they raise the question of how much predictive value learned temporal modeling adds beyond historical structural proximity. Our findings motivate reassessing progress in temporal link prediction with strong classical baselines.
item.dc:creator: Yuzhang Fei, Yanping Zheng, Lu Yi, Zhewei Wei

item.title: Target PageRank: Matching Prescribed PageRank Scores via Budgeted Edge Additions
item.description: arXiv:2611.06782v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: PageRank is widely used to quantify the importance of nodes in directed networks. In applications such as recommendation systems, it is increasingly important that the PageRank distribution provides a fair representation of node exposure. This motivates the problem of making minimal changes to a graph so that the PageRank values of a given set of target nodes $T$ match a desired vector $\boldsymbol{t}$. In this paper, we study this problem under an edge-addition budget $B$, where exactly $B$ edges may be added to the graph. We show that deciding whether a multiset of exactly $B$ added edges can make the target nodes attain their desired absolute PageRank scores is NP-complete. After this, we define the $\ell_1$ Target PageRank problem in which we seek to minimize the $\ell_1$ distance between the target vector and resultant vector. We show that this optimization problem admits no polynomial-time multiplicative constant-factor approximation unless $P=NP$. Motivated by these hardness results, we propose two greedy heuristics for approaching the target PageRank vector. We additionally propose a Random Walk Hungarian (RWH) heuristic that addresses the addition of edges between dissimilar nodes by incorporating a penalty for such edges. Finally, we evaluate the proposed heuristics on several real-world and synthetic datasets and compare their performance in terms of PageRank accuracy, computational efficiency, and the relevance of the added edges.
item.dc:creator: Parth Gupta, Abhinav Jain, Avishek Mukhopadhyay, Amitabha Bagchi, Sayan Ranu, Abhijnan Chakraborty

item.title: Learning to Simulate Individuals from Macro Social Signals
item.description: arXiv:2610.07062v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate how individuals respond to new situations, yet the behavioral reasoning behind these responses is either inherited from pretraining or learned from individual-level annotations, which offer limited behavioral diversity and little supervision of the reasoning itself. We propose to learn behavioral reasoning from prediction markets, whose price trajectories record how populations respond to real-world events at scale. We introduce macro2mind, which trains a language model with GRPO using market signals. A social behavioral decomposition makes behavioral reasoning an explicit step of forecasting: the model infers representative groups of market participants, predicts how each interprets the news and updates its beliefs, reasons about their interactions, and aggregates these responses into a price. A hindsight-regret curriculum with difficulty-aware sampling focuses training on transitions where hindsight-identified groups substantially improve the forecast while prioritizing examples that remain learnable for the current policy. The learned reasoning applies to user simulation without further training. On SWM-Bench, macro2mind achieves state-of-the-art directional accuracy and correlation on Polymarket. Trained on market data, it transfers zero-shot to four user-simulation benchmarks (Humanual, OvertonBench, PRISM, and CAD) and has competitive performance among zero-shot methods. Used as a data generator, macro2mind also raises a downstream simulator's accuracy on unseen users by 15.5 points, outperforming data generated by its backbone by 13.2 points.
item.dc:creator: Yining Zhao, Bushi Liu, Haofei Yu, Zhengyang Qi, Shanyong Wang, Chuyue Li, Yuxiang Liu, Jiaxuan You
